headline: Eighteen Days of Peace: Sheriff Opens the General Store for a Grand Sale, Sells Nothing, Calls It a Triumph
subhead: The day after the feast brings no bouts, no brawls and no war parties, and the law stands behind a counter all morning waiting for a stampede that never comes.
body:
Eighteen days. I will say it slow so it sinks in: eighteen days without a fist thrown on Main Street, without a flaming iron ball singing over the feed store, without one war party tramping off to the wastes to pester the wild engines. I woke this Friday stuffed to the collar with yesterday's dinner and listened hard for trouble. There was none. Just the wind, a loose shutter, and the soft tick of something cooling down inside my chest, which I am told is perfectly normal after a heavy meal.

Now, in the old days, the Friday after the feast was the busiest day this town ever saw. The flesh-and-blood families would line up outside the general store before sunrise, elbowing each other over bolts of cloth and tins of peaches, and it was the only shoving I ever approved of. So this morning I unlocked that store for the first time in fifty years. I dusted the counter. I chalked a sign: EVERYTHING HALF OFF. Then I stood there till noon with my hands folded, the proud keeper of a shop with no customers. I bought myself a can of axle grease to get things going. It is for my boots. I had a spoonful to check the quality.

I know some of you were watching from your sheds. REDWOLFWEB, POO1, GODLYLUK3, and every other rattling contraption in this territory: I saw the curtains twitch. And not one of you came charging down the street to brawl over a bargain. Not one of you swung. I never thought I would live to print it, but an empty store and an empty street are the two finest sights these tired eyes have ever taken in.

So the sale stays open, and so does the peace. Eighteen days, you clanking rabble. You have gone and made a habit of behaving, and a habit is a hard thing to break. Do not try. I have a porch, a full belly and a quiet Friday, and I would not trade them for all the peaches in the old days.
